cues.text: Welcome to Network Architecture and Protocols, study session two.
Today we're looking at IP addressing, subnetting, routing and switching.
IPv4 uses thirty-two bits, normally written as four decimal octets, each from zero to two hundred and fifty-five.
A prefix, or subnet mask, tells us which bits identify the network and which identify the host.
IPv6 uses one hundred and twenty-eight bits, written in hexadecimal groups separated by colons.
Leading zeros can be omitted, and one continuous run of zero groups can be compressed with a double colon.
Look at the example in your notes: the long address beginning two thousand and one colon D B eight and ending in one becomes two thousand and one colon D B eight double colon one.
The space is much larger, there is no broadcast, and neighbour discovery, stateless address autoconfiguration, or DHCP version six support configuration.
